name: Napoleon
info: Napoleon Bonaparte was a Corsican-born general of the French Revolution who became First Consul in 1799 and was Emperor of the French from 1804 to 1814 and again in 1815, leading campaigns across Europe and enacting lasting legal reforms.

facts.born: 15 August 1769 at the Maison Bonaparte in Ajaccio, Corsica; son of Carlo Maria Buonaparte and Maria Letizia Ramolino, of a family of Italian origin descended from minor Tuscan nobility
facts.died: 5 May 1821 on the island of Saint Helena, in British custody, at age 51; two autopsy reports concluded that he died of internal bleeding caused by stomach cancer
facts.role: Brigadier general after the capture of Toulon in December 1793; head of the Army of Italy from 1796; First Consul from 1799, consul for life from 1802; Emperor of the French from 18 May 1804 to April 1814 and during the Hundred Days of 1815; King of Italy from 1805
facts.known: the Coup of 18 Brumaire; the Napoleonic Code; the Concordat of 1801; the victory at Austerlitz; the invasion of Russia in 1812; the defeat at Waterloo; the reinstatement of slavery in French colonies; exile on Saint Helena

t: A Corsican artillery officer who rose through the wars of the French Revolution, Napoleon seized power in the coup of November 1799 and crowned himself Emperor of the French in December 1804.

His victories from Austerlitz to Wagram brought about 40% of Europe's population under his direct or indirect rule, while his civil code, prefects, lycées and Concordat reshaped France; he also ended the free press and reinstated slavery in French colonies.

The war in Spain and the invasion of Russia in 1812 broke his power: he abdicated in 1814, returned for the Hundred Days, was defeated at Waterloo in June 1815 and died a British prisoner on Saint Helena.
dyk: During the Napoleonic Wars the British press mocked Napoleon as a short-tempered small man, nicknamed "Little Boney". In fact, at about 168 cm (5 ft 6 in), he was of average height.
ev: Napoleon is born in Ajaccio, Corsica, one year after the Republic of Genoa ceded the island to France
As artillery commander he plans the assault that recaptures the port of Toulon and is promoted to brigadier general
After campaigns in Italy and Egypt he overthrows the Directory in the Coup of 18 Brumaire and becomes First Consul
His civil code is implemented in March; the senate proclaims him Emperor of the French in May and he crowns himself at Notre Dame in December
He defeats the Austrian and Russian armies at the Battle of Austerlitz, weeks after the British naval victory at Trafalgar
He invades Russia with around 450,000 frontline troops, occupies Moscow and loses most of his army in the retreat
Escaping from exile on Elba, he retakes power for the Hundred Days, is defeated at Waterloo and is sent to Saint Helena
Napoleon dies on Saint Helena at the age of 51

sections.early:
Napoleon was born on 15 August 1769 in the Maison Bonaparte in Ajaccio, Corsica, and baptized Napoleone di Buonaparte. His family was of Italian origin: his father's ancestors descended from a minor Tuscan noble family that emigrated to Corsica in the 16th century, his mother's from a noble family of Lombardy. He was the second of the eight surviving children of Carlo Maria Buonaparte and Maria Letizia Ramolino. He was born one year after the Republic of Genoa ceded Corsica to France. His father had supported Pasquale Paoli in the Corsican war of independence, but after the Corsican defeat in 1769 he became friends with the French governor, Charles Louis de Marbeuf, with whose support Napoleon obtained a royal bursary to a military academy in mainland France.

In January 1779, aged 9, he moved to the mainland, first to a religious school in Autun to improve his French, his mother tongues being Corsican and Italian, and in May to the military academy at Brienne-le-Château. There he was routinely bullied for his accent, birthplace, short stature and poor French; he became reserved and melancholic and applied himself to reading.

In September 1784 he was admitted to the École militaire in Paris to train as an artillery officer. His father's death in February 1785 cut the family income and forced him to complete the two-year course in one. In September 1785 he became the first Corsican to graduate from the school and was commissioned a second lieutenant in La Fère artillery regiment.
sections.rise:
Bonaparte supported the Revolution of 1789 and promoted its cause in Corsica, where he joined the pro-French republicans against Paoli; in 1793 the Buonapartes fled to Toulon. That September he was appointed artillery commander of the republican forces sent to recapture the port, and his plan to take a hill fort dominating the harbour led to the city's capture in December. After the fall of Maximilien Robespierre in July 1794 his Jacobin connections made him suspect, and he was arrested for two weeks.

On 5 October 1795, 13 Vendémiaire, he defended the National Convention against a royalist rebellion in Paris, firing on the rebels with canister rounds; about 300 to 1,400 rebels died. The new government, the Directory, made him head of the Army of Italy in January 1796. On 9 March he married Joséphine de Beauharnais. In Italy he knocked the Piedmontese out of the war in two weeks and defeated every Austrian effort to relieve Mantua; the victory at Rivoli in January 1797 led to the Treaty of Campo Formio, and he returned to Paris a hero.

In 1798 he led an expedition to Egypt and won the Battle of the Pyramids on 21 July, but on 1 August the British fleet under Horatio Nelson destroyed the French fleet. He left his army in August 1799 without explicit orders. On 9 November 1799, 18 Brumaire, he and his allies overthrew the Directory, and the Constitution of the Year VIII gave real power to Bonaparte as First Consul. The plebiscite that approved it officially counted over three million in favour, his brother Lucien having doubled the "yes" vote.
sections.deeds:
The victory at Marengo on 14 June 1800 increased Bonaparte's authority, and the Treaty of Amiens with Britain in March 1802 brought a decade of war to an end. By the Concordat of 1801 Pope Pius VII recognized his regime and the regime recognized Catholicism as the majority religion of France. A plebiscite in 1802 made him consul for life. He established prefects to run the departments, the Council of State, the Banque de France, secondary schools and lycées, and the Legion of Honour. His civil code, implemented in March 1804 and known from 1807 as the Napoleonic Code, entrenched equality before the law, religious toleration, secure property rights and the abolition of the vestiges of feudalism.

On 18 May 1804 the senate proclaimed him Emperor of the French, and on 2 December, at Notre Dame de Paris, he crowned himself after being anointed by the pope. In 1805 he captured 60,000 Austrian soldiers at Ulm and on 2 December defeated the Austrians and Russians at Austerlitz, where about a third of the allied forces were killed, captured or wounded. The Confederation of the Rhine, established in 1806, spelled the end of the Holy Roman Empire.

He defeated Prussia at Jena and Auerstedt on 14 October 1806 and Russia at Friedland on 14 June 1807; by the Treaties of Tilsit Prussia lost half its territory and population. He placed his brothers on the thrones of Naples, Holland, Westphalia and Spain, and after the Battle of Wagram in July 1809 he ruled about 40% of the European population, directly or through satellite kingdoms.
sections.opponents:
A succession of coalitions of European powers fought France, and Britain declared war again in May 1803; after Trafalgar his fleet never again seriously challenged the Royal Navy. His installation of his brother Joseph as King of Spain in 1808 provoked an uprising met with brutal French repression and a guerrilla war in which both sides committed atrocities; Napoleon later called it "the unlucky war [that] ruined me". Pope Pius VII excommunicated him in 1809 and was arrested and held until 1814.

At home he introduced censorship, closed most opposition newspapers and ended directly elected representative government. In 1804 he had the Duke of Enghien kidnapped and executed after a secret trial, though there was no proof of his involvement in a royalist plot. In May 1802 he reintroduced slavery in the recovered colonies, and the expedition he sent to retake Saint-Domingue failed; the former slaves proclaimed the republic of Haiti in 1804. At Jaffa in 1799 he ordered the garrison and some 1,500–5,000 prisoners to be executed.

Critics cite his exploitation of conquered territories and the plunder of art for the Louvre. Historians have argued that his expansionist foreign policy was a major factor in the Napoleonic wars, which cost six million lives. Frank McLynn and Correlli Barnett suggest that his reputation as a military genius is exaggerated. Pieter Geyl in 1947 and Claude Ribbe in 2005 compared him to Adolf Hitler; most modern critics reject the comparison, arguing that he did not commit genocide or the mass murder of his political opponents.
sections.last:
On 24 June 1812 Napoleon's multinational Grande Armée, around 450,000 frontline troops, began crossing into Russia. After the Battle of Borodino on 7 September, which left 44,000 Russian and 35,000 French dead, wounded or captured, he entered Moscow, but Tsar Alexander refused to negotiate and after six weeks the army withdrew through cold, disease and hunger. About 75,000 troops recrossed the Nieman; total military deaths on both sides were up to one million. In 1813 Prussia and Austria joined Russia, and the coalition won the Battle of Leipzig in October. The allies entered France, Paris capitulated on 31 March 1814, and Napoleon abdicated unconditionally on 6 April.

Exiled to Elba, he escaped on 26 February 1815 with about 1,000 men, was joined by the troops sent to stop him and entered Paris on 20 March. The powers declared him an outlaw. On 18 June Wellington's army withstood his attacks at Waterloo until Blücher's Prussians arrived on his right flank. He abdicated on 22 June in favour of his son, whom the allies refused to recognize, and on 15 July surrendered to the British on HMS Bellerophon.

He was held on Saint Helena in the Atlantic, at Longwood House, a damp and unhealthy bungalow, guarded by 2,100 soldiers. His health worsened from mid-1817, and he died on 5 May 1821 at age 51. Two autopsy reports concluded that he died of internal bleeding caused by stomach cancer; a later theory of arsenic poisoning was undermined by further studies. In 1840 his remains were returned to France, and in 1861 they were entombed at Les Invalides.
sections.legacy:
Napoleon's reforms outlasted him. The Napoleonic Code, carried across Europe by his armies, continued to influence the law in western Europe, Latin America, Louisiana and Quebec; Alfred Cobban called it "the most effective agency for the propagation of the basic principles of the French Revolution". His regime abolished remnants of feudalism in conquered lands, closed the Jewish ghettos and ended the Spanish Inquisition. His schools laid the foundation of modern secondary and tertiary education in France.

His reorganization of Germany and his rule in Italy sparked nationalism and the movements toward German and Italian unification, and the ousting of the Spanish Bourbons indirectly began the process of Latin American independence. His reputation is generally favourable in Poland, the only country to evoke him in its national anthem.

A legend grew from his own propaganda and from The Memorial of Saint Helena, published by Las Cases in 1822, which presented him as a liberal deposed by reactionaries. It fed defiance of the restored Bourbons, and David A. Bell argues that the regime of Napoleon III was possible only because of it. Historians remain divided on whether he was "an enlightened despot who laid the foundations of modern Europe" or "a megalomaniac who wrought greater misery than any man before the coming of Hitler". Carl von Clausewitz regarded him as a genius in the art of war. Pieter Geyl wrote in 1947 that it is impossible for two historians, especially of different periods, to see any historical personality in the same light.

summary: Napoleon Bonaparte rose from Corsican artillery officer to First Consul of France in 1799 and Emperor of the French in 1804. He defeated the armies of Austria, Prussia and Russia and gave France its civil code, but the war in Spain and the invasion of Russia in 1812 led to his abdication in 1814. Defeated at Waterloo in 1815, he died in exile on Saint Helena in 1821.
references: David A. Bell, Napoleon: A Concise Biography (Oxford University Press, 2015)
Rafe Blaufarb, Napoleon: Symbol for an Age, A Brief History with Documents (Bedford, 2008)
Michael Broers, Napoleon: Soldier of Destiny (Faber and Faber, 2015)
Michael Broers, Napoleon: The Decline and Fall of an Empire, 1811–1821 (Pegasus books, 2022)
notes: References are from the article's Further reading list; its Works cited headings are empty in the saved file. The article abbreviates 'Oxford U.P.'; written out here.

Jaffa: the article's narrative says 'some 1,500-5,000 prisoners' were executed; its Criticism section says Bell and McLynn condemn 'his killing of 3,000-5,000 Turkish prisoners of war in Syria'. The profile uses the first figure.
13 Vendémiaire: 'About 300 to 1,400 rebels died' is the article's range.

The article gives no date for the promotion to brigadier general beyond 'Toulon brought Bonaparte to the attention of powerful men ... He was promoted' (assault of 16-17 December 1793; artillery commander of the Army of Italy in February 1794).
The emperor's end date: the senate declared him deposed on 2 April 1814 and he abdicated unconditionally on 6 April; the lead says 'until his first abdication in 1814'. 'role' says April 1814.
The brothers on thrones: Joseph (Naples 1806, Spain 1808), Louis (Holland 1806), Jérôme (Westphalia 1807), all from the article.

The 1812 event says he 'loses most of his army': from the article's figures (around 450,000 frontline troops at the start; about 75,000 recrossed the Nieman). The article does not give a single total for French losses.

'Undermined by further studies' summarises the article on the arsenic theory (arsenic also found in childhood hair samples and those of his son and Joséphine; a 2021 study again concluded stomach cancer).
'Genius' appears only in judgements the article attributes (McLynn and Barnett; Clausewitz).

Left out for space: the First Italian campaign's plunder figures (45 million French pounds, more than 300 works of art), the Syrian campaign's losses, the Louisiana context, the marriages to Joséphine and Marie Louise and the birth of the King of Rome in 1811, the Continental System, religious emancipation of the Jews, the psychological theories.
